ABOUT THIS EDITION

The Igbo Contemporary Bible (Baịbụlụ Nsọ nʼIgbo Ndị Ugbu a) is a modern Igbo-language Bible translation published by Biblica. Igbo is a Volta-Niger language of southeastern Nigeria. The copyright dates of 1980, 1988, 2019, and 2020 indicate a multi-decade translation and revision process. The initial work was done under Living Bibles International (LBI), which had established Living Bibles Nigeria to produce contemporary Scripture translations in Nigerian languages; LBI merged with the International Bible Society in 1992 to form what is now Biblica. The Igbo Living Bible New Testament was first published in 1988. The translation was subsequently revised and expanded into a full Bible, with the most recent update in 2020. The earlier Union Igbo Bible, translated by British Anglican missionary Thomas John Dennis and completed by 1913, had long been the standard Igbo Bible but was criticized — notably by novelist Chinua Achebe — for its impact on the Igbo language, contributing to demand for a contemporary translation. The Igbo Contemporary Bible is released under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 license and is available digitally through YouVersion and Biblica's website.

he 1905 Igbo Genesis is a scripture portion printed by the British and Foreign Bible Society at London during the preparation of the first complete Igbo Bible, Union Igbo, which appeared in 1913. Igbo, a Benue-Congo language spoken by more than thirty million people across southeastern Nigeria, had by the early twentieth century accumulated a quarter-century of Church Missionary Society publishing, but the extreme dialectal variation between Onitsha, Owerri, Aba, and Arochukwu forms had prevented any single dialect from becoming a useable ecclesiastical standard.

The Onitsha gospels of Bishop Samuel Ajayi Crowther and his son Dandeson Crowther appeared between 1873 and 1892, and the full Onitsha New Testament was printed by BFBS in 1900. Translator Thomas John Dennis, who had arrived at Onitsha in 1893, recognized that the Onitsha-dialect text was not adequately understood in Owerri and Ngwa country and set out to create an artificial pan-Igbo literary register drawn from several dialects. Working with a team of Igbo assistants at the CMS station at Onitsha and later at Obosi, Dennis translated Genesis and other Old Testament books during 1902 to 1905 and had them printed as individual portions by the BFBS for use and testing while the full Bible manuscript was being prepared.

The 1905 Genesis represents one of those portions.

he 1906 Igbo Job through Malachi completes the Old Testament prophetic and poetic books in what the Church Missionary Society styled the Union Igbo translation, printed by the British and Foreign Bible Society in London. Thomas John Dennis (1869–1917), a CMS missionary stationed at Onitsha from 1893, led the committee formed in 1905 that sought to produce a single written Igbo accepted across the major dialect regions of Onitsha, Owerri, Arochukwu, Bonny, and Umuahia. The Union text drew lexical and grammatical decisions from all five, a compromise that provoked opposition from some Igbo readers who preferred their local speech in Scripture.

Earlier Igbo Scripture had appeared in the Isuama dialect through the work of Samuel Ajayi Crowther and John Christopher Taylor from the 1860s, but those editions were judged inadequate for general circulation. Dennis shipped drafts from Onitsha to London for printing with types cast for African-language diacritics, then distributed the bound portions back through the Niger River mission stations.

The 1906 poetic and prophetic books followed the 1903 Gospels, 1905 Acts and Epistles, and 1906 earlier Old Testament portions. Dennis was lost at sea in 1917 on the SS Karina before completing the full Bible, which was finished by his colleagues and issued as the Union Igbo Bible in 1913.

his 1982 Genesis portion in Igbo was issued by the Bible Society of Nigeria as part of the standard Igbo Scripture program serving roughly 30 million speakers in southeastern Nigeria. Igbo is a Volta-Niger language of the Niger-Congo family, the language of the peoples of Anambra, Imo, Abia, Enugu, Ebonyi, and parts of Delta and Rivers states, with substantial Igbo-speaking populations throughout Nigeria and in the global diaspora.

The Igbo Bible has a distinguished translation history. Early Scripture portions were produced by the Church Missionary Society beginning in the 1840s; the Isuama Igbo Gospels appeared in the 1850s under Samuel Ajayi Crowther, the liberated Yoruba slave who became the first African Anglican bishop. A Union Igbo New Testament prepared by a committee under T. J. Dennis appeared in 1900, and the complete Union Igbo Bible, called Bible Nsọ, was published in 1913. The Union version became the liturgical standard of the Anglican and Methodist churches, though its heavily standardized idiom was not universally welcomed.

A modern Igbo Bible, Baịbụlụ Nsọ Nhazi Ọhụrụ (the New Revised Edition), was released in more recent decades. This 1982 Genesis portion represents an intermediate publication for church and literacy use, circulating alongside the full Bible. The Bible Society of Nigeria, headquartered in Lagos, has coordinated distribution nationwide.

his printed Igbo Bible is part of the distribution history of the Union Igbo Bible, the standard scripture edition produced by the Church Missionary Society and the British and Foreign Bible Society for the Igbo-speaking peoples of southeastern Nigeria. Igbo (ISO 639-3 ibo) is a Volta-Niger language of the Niger-Congo family with over 30 million speakers, the principal language of Abia, Anambra, Ebonyi, Enugu, and Imo states, with significant populations in Rivers and Delta states.

The Union Igbo Bible was coordinated by Thomas John Dennis of the CMS at Onitsha between 1905 and 1913, with the Pentateuch appearing in 1909 and the complete Bible published by BFBS in 1913. Dennis worked with a committee of Igbo and European translators to produce what he called Union Igbo, a deliberately synthetic literary form drawing on features of Onitsha, Owerri, Arochukwu, Bonny, and Unwana dialects. The project was controversial: some Igbo speakers preferred dialect-specific translations, and Union Igbo was criticized for being nobody's mother tongue. Nonetheless the Dennis Bible became the ecclesial standard, reinforcing Igbo literary unity for a century.

Subsequent Igbo translations include the Catholic Nsọ Bible, the Living Bible in Igbo, the Central Igbo Bible of 1988, and the contemporary Igbo Revised Version of 2007. The Dennis Union Igbo, however, remains in print and is reissued by the Bible Society of Nigeria for continued congregational use.

his Gospel of John in Igbo is a Bible Society of Nigeria edition in the standard literary Igbo used since the 1913 Union Igbo Bible. Igbo is a Volta-Niger language of the Niger-Congo family, spoken by roughly 30 million people across southeastern Nigeria, principally in Abia, Anambra, Ebonyi, Enugu, and Imo states, with extensive diaspora communities in Nigeria's other regions and abroad.

The Igbo Bible tradition begins with Samuel Ajayi Crowther's Niger Mission, which produced the first Gospel of Matthew (Isoama-Ibo) in 1860 and extended to a full translation effort under the Church Missionary Society. The Union Igbo Bible of 1913, prepared by Thomas Dennis and a committee drawing on multiple dialects, established a supra-dialectal literary Igbo that shaped written Igbo in education and church through the twentieth century. The Union Igbo remained the predominant ecclesiastical text into the 1980s, when the Bible Society of Nigeria issued a revised "Nsọ Bible" in contemporary standard Igbo.

This John edition is one of the single-Gospel portions issued by BSN for evangelism, literacy, and Sunday School use, printed as a lightweight paperback in standard Igbo orthography with tone diacritics and the subdot vowels (ị, ọ, ụ) that distinguish Igbo typography. It circulated through the Anglican, Methodist, Presbyterian, Catholic, and Pentecostal churches that together form the overwhelmingly Christian Igbo heartland. The present edition follows the modern BSN Igbo text rather than the 1913 Union Igbo.

ew Testament in Igbo, a Volta-Niger (Benue-Congo) language spoken by over 30 million people in the five Igbo-majority states of southeastern Nigeria and by diaspora Igbo communities worldwide. Igbo is written in a Latin-based orthography with tone marks, standardized in the 20th century through the Onwu Committee and officially adopted in 1961.

Igbo Scripture has a layered history. Samuel Ajayi Crowther, the liberated Yoruba convert and first African bishop of the Anglican communion, collaborated with the Church Missionary Society on early Igbo translations from Isuama and Onitsha dialects in the 1850s and 1860s. Julius Spencer and Thomas John Dennis revised the Onitsha Igbo New Testament, which appeared complete in 1900, and the first full Igbo Bible (Bible Nso) was published in 1913 in a composite literary dialect known as Union Igbo, shaped by Dennis to bridge the major regional forms (Oraka 1983; Sanneh 2009).

A second translation in standard modern Igbo, Baibulu Nso Nhazi Ohuru (the New Revised Version), was published in 2007 by the Bible Society of Nigeria after a three-decade revision process aligned with the official Onwu orthography. This New Testament print circulates in one of these revised forms and is distributed by the Bible Society of Nigeria through Anglican, Catholic, Methodist, and Pentecostal churches in Aba, Onitsha, Owerri, Enugu, and Umuahia, as well as through Igbo-language chaplaincies in Lagos and abroad.
